work.title: Homily on Palm Sunday and on Lazarus

paragraphs.text: A sermon by Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, for Palm Sunday and on Lazarus. When the church trumpets forth the children crying, “Hosanna in the highest,” and I draw that radiant, godly cry to myself, I will be lifted high in my zeal. For it is dreadful if a barren nature overcomes joy; but love does not know how to wait for the time that summons it. And in my swift mind I go about Bethany, clapping my hands and rejoicing. And I mingle with the children and leap with them, joining them in raising a song of victory to the Master: “Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” And again, when I see them carrying branches and meeting Christ, forming choirs and spreading their garments, I rejoice

likewise when I see the children, with a simple tongue and [?], making a song for the King. But then I am moved still more to weep over and hate the wickedness of the Jews. For the children show understanding, while the fathers prepare themselves for murder; and the infants speak of God, while the fathers set themselves against God. Then I also see the fallen wisdom of the scribes themselves. For, having wickedly exalted themselves through the glory and pretense of understanding, from true and divine wisdom they have indeed fallen away. Then I also lament their teachers for the hardness of their hearts, because, though entrusted with teaching others, through their own wickedness they were not worthy even to stand in the same rank as their own pupils. And those who had promised to heal the sickness of others were themselves sick with the ultimate sickness, madness, having grievously wounded their whole soul with the passion of pride, and with a truly double wound they suffered. For, being wicked and suffering grievously, they could not fail to feel their own suffering. For they ought to have welcomed the physician when he came and was among them, pouring out rivers of healing for them, and easily and without food, through him who washed them, to have cleansed their stains and washed away their passions. But, willfully and wickedly blinding both their senses and their mind together, they turned away from their own healing, and their Savior and Creator

they did not wish to recognize. For, as Saint Paul said, had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. They did not understand, for they did not even know how to desire it. For where the will is opposed, then the mind is taken captive by the passion that holds it; and the mind’s freedom, though called to the good, does not attain an understanding of the truth. They did not recognize him who is glorified by angels and proclaimed by prophets. They did not recognize him who sits at the Father’s right hand and is carried on a virgin’s arm, and sets things in motion with a single word. They did not recognize him who sits upon the throne of the cherubim, and is carried on a donkey’s colt, and is praised by children, and came to suffer willingly. They neither recognized him nor chose to understand. Instead, claiming to be wise, they became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened in their thoughts. This prophet spoke long beforehand, foreseeing: “They hear but do not understand, and though they look, they do not see. For the heart of these people has grown dull, and their ears have become hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn back so that I may heal them.” Tell me, then, O Jew, why do you boast of the prophets, yet revile him whom they prophesied? How can you pore over books while disregarding the meaning of what is written? And you gather the shoots

of the law, but neglect to gather the true clusters of grapes. And in the mines of the scriptures you [?] in vain, but you neither dig out nor gather the gold hidden in them. But others, having lovingly gathered a flower from the blossoms of the law, radiant and brightly [?], rejoice in the Church’s bridal chamber, and bear what gives off a sweet fragrance in grace— godliness. But you, having covered your eyes with leaves, have given yourself entirely to that place, neither feeling distress at that dense growth nor turning your face to look at the blossom. And you wickedly multiply the pearls of hell with which they adorn themselves. But Christ’s people, uncovering it fittingly, truly receive a pure and genuine radiance. And you sit at the bridal chamber, having labored for a long time, yet you do not welcome the bridegroom who has come, held captive by lust for fornication, having truly gathered [?], without manliness, and alone among orphaned words, without understanding. Truly these people are foolish and not wise. For from the beginning they were chosen for the law, nor were they ranked last in the knowledge of God. Have you not heard King David singing under God’s inspiration: “Out of the mouths of nursing infants you have perfected praise, because of your enemies”? Do you not believe

Believe the prophet as a kinsman, if you have not renounced your kinship in words as well. For I have long known that you have renounced him by your deeds. Even if you disregard him as a shepherd, fear him as a king. For, being a king, he knows how to threaten if he perceives anyone being negligent or angry. He will bring a flashing spear against them and shepherd them with an iron rod, and like clay vessels he will shatter the things fashioned by a corrupt mind. Say with him in a loud voice: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.” The Savior has come, wishing to take vengeance on your understanding. Wishing to take vengeance on yours, he establishes the praise of infants. Why do you begrudge your own salvation? Why are you so unwilling to receive a kindness? Even if this too seems evil to you, it is for your good. Nevertheless, he will overcome your malice. Do you refuse to heed what you hear? Then heed what can be seen. Do you not believe the prophet Isaiah, who cries out and says: “Tongues will learn to speak peace concerning him”? Do not tongues plainly speak the truth concerning him? Have the children of the world not learned to offer praise? For Christ is our peace, who tore down the dividing wall of hostility, and through whom, after previously falling away wickedly, we were reconciled with the Father and Creator

again. Did not Zechariah, through the Holy Spirit, proclaim this joy to Zion beforehand, saying, “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem! Look, your king is coming to you, righteous and bringing salvation. He is gentle and mounted on a donkey, on a donkey’s colt.” Do you not have your own eyes as witnesses to what was foretold? Have you not heard what was prophesied? You see that very thing standing before you. Has the deed not come together with the words? Is he not gentle? Is he not righteous? Does he not bring salvation? Has he not mounted a donkey? Do not tongues clearly proclaim peace concerning him? Do not children offer him praise, possessing the understanding of elders? Children offer praise so that he may expose all envy as empty words of hostility. For even someone wishing to act maliciously [?] some cunning and a desire to please in this life, those who offer praise and glorify the Master will be spared. For the nature of children knows neither cunning nor deceit, nor is it enslaved to the passion for flattery, but just as the gift of the Holy Spirit puts it into their ears. Thus this man places the gift of the Holy Spirit into their ears, into their ears. Thus they praise the miracle. Children bring gifts, so that everyone, through deeds,

may learn that it is not those who have a [?] mind, and are fond of disputes and wish to incur shame, to whom the mysterious gift is given. Rather, it is those who approach with a pure mind and an innocent heart. To them the understanding of godliness is revealed. For that which is beyond investigation— if anyone insists on investigating it, rather than following the holy words, then even nature’s [?] and the words in which he boasts he will grievously tear apart, and he will revile the law of theology. And he will revile his [?], and lose the holiness he investigates. Children offer praise, so that they may expose their parents’ lawlessness and renew the knowledge of God among believers. For whatever surpasses the mind [?], and they learn improperly through thought [?]. Much [?] knows [?]; holy [?] is needed. But that which dwells in pure hearts without defilement reveals true understanding to others through them. But do you not see Lazarus risen from the tomb, the dead man among the living, reclining at supper with the Lord? Yet you untie the dead man’s burial wrappings, but do not undo your own unbelief. And you roll away the tombstone, but you do not cast out the envy from your soul, which produces worse pus for you. And you see Hades, at the Lord’s

command, giving up the man who had been dead for four days. Yet, to murder the very one who raised him, you sharpen the hands that killed the prophets. Oh, what exceedingly great folly! Oh, what exceedingly great, incurable hardness of heart! Have they turned their minds to such lawlessness that they do not believe because of the very things that should have led them to believe? They revile him for the very things for which they should praise him. For the things for which they should glorify and magnify him, they do not call him blessed. For the things for which they should sing and give thanks, they condemn him and become fighters against God. Such is the madness of both groups. Such is their [?] restraint. For [?], having intoxicated their minds with delusion and [?], does not allow the mind’s eye to see through the darkness poured over it, or to look upon the rays of truth. Such is the sickness of the Pharisees and scribes, who prize the foremost places at feasts and take pride in being called teachers, and boast of the breadth of their fringes, imagining that they are keeping the Law. having no truth in them at all, and speaking not a single word of godliness. Such is the sting of envy: once it has driven envy deep into the soul, it wounds the whole person. It destroys the ability to care for what is good, and the senses, which are the most necessary

pathways to learning, it drives away most cruelly, neither allowing one to understand what is fitting nor strengthening what one hears through memory, nor allowing one to see visible things clearly. But let us, beloved, flee these passions that harm the soul. Let us flee arrogance, because of which the leader of the bodiless powers fell at the beginning. Let us flee envy, if for no other reason than that it harms the one who practices it, even if it causes little distress to the person he envies. Let us flee arrogance and glory, by which the understanding of truth is driven away. Let us flee ingratitude and blasphemy. For these drove the chief priests and the Jewish scribes into a frenzy to murder Christ. This made the chief priests and scribes more foolish than infants. Let us not imitate the foolishness of the Jews, but emulate the children’s thanksgiving, not the elders’ [?], but the infants’ praise of God; not the ignorance of the envious, but the knowledge of God shown by those who praise him; not the hostility of murderers, but the innocence of the young. Let us also become like children, for the Lord said, “Unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Let us be children without malice,

inscribing nothing evil or cruel upon the soul, but with complete purity and without any mark of evil, receiving and inscribing the godly faith, so that we may enter the kingdom of heaven. Let us bring the Lord branches of mercy and love for humanity, so that we may enter the kingdom of heaven. Let us meet him as he comes riding on a colt, exposing the foolishness of the Jews and granting holiness to the nations. Let us meet him, spreading cloaks. How? By spreading them for the poor. For he himself took poverty upon himself and cries out, “Inasmuch as you did it to one of these least of my brothers, you did it to me.” Oh, what a loving and holy voice! “You spread cloaks for me,” he says, “when you clothe the poor. You warm me when you relieve them of bitter cold and suffering.” We spread our cloaks for him, so that with the children we may cry out for deliverance. Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is he who comes to stretch out his hands on the cross and gather the nations to himself. Blessed is he who comes to show Hades bound, to release Adam from his bonds, and to raise up the fallen. Blessed is he

who comes. He will crush the power of torment and, coming in the last days, grant forgiveness. Blessed is he who comes. He will empty the dwellings of Hades, but the heavenly dwellings he will fill with many who are being saved. Blessed is he who comes. He will offer himself as a sacrifice for us, and cleanse all sins and reconcile us with the Father. Blessed is he who comes to curse death and renew resurrection for us. He will free us from slavery and grant us adoption as God's children. For this belongs to you, Lord, who created us and brought us into being from nothing and fashioned us, and, when we have fallen, once more, and when we have been broken, to raise us up and reshape us. This belongs to your love for humankind: to seek out the one who has gone astray and turn him back from error, and make him worthy of his original place. For we are your people and the sheep of your pasture, and we all rely on you, and we give you glory and thanks, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the Trinity, one in essence, life-giving, and almighty, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
